hook: Orchard A grows heavier apples on average than orchard B, by 10 grams. A buyer weighs 40 apples from A and 50 from B. Could her sample from B still come out heavier? To answer, you need the sampling distribution of a difference: where $\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B$ centers, how much it varies, and its shape.

prereq.q: For random samples of size $n$ (under 10% of the population), the standard deviation of $\bar{x}$ is
prereq.why: $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$; its square, $\frac{\sigma^2}{n}$, is the variance of $\bar{x}$.

prereq.q: For two independent samples, the standard deviation of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ is
prereq.why: The two variances add, then take the square root.

figure.caption: Top: the sampling distributions of $\bar{x}_A$ (mean 180, SD 3.16) and $\bar{x}_B$ (mean 170, SD 3.54). Bottom: the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B$, centered at 10 with SD 4.74, wider than either. The shaded area, 0.0175, is the chance that B's sample mean comes out larger.

chain.cause: Each sample mean is centered at its population mean
Each sample mean has its own variability, $\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1}$ and $\frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}$
chain.effect: for independent samples the variances add, so the difference varies more than either mean

chain.cause: Take the square root of the sum
If each sample mean is approximately normal (normal population or $n \ge 30$ for each)
chain.effect: the difference is approximately normal, and z-scores give probabilities

ideas: Spread: $\sigma_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}$ for independent samples (or groups formed by random assignment), each under 10% of its population when sampling.
Variances add, never standard deviations, and never subtract.
Shape: normal if both populations are normal; approximately normal if both $n_1 \ge 30$ and $n_2 \ge 30$.

misconception.wrong: The means are subtracted, so the variability of the difference is the first variance minus the second.
misconception.right: Both sample means wobble, and both wobbles end up in the difference. For independent samples the variances add: $\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}$.

summary: For independent random samples (or randomly assigned groups), $\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2$ has mean $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}$, and it is approximately normal when each sample mean is. Use $z = \frac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - (\mu_1 - \mu_2)}{\sigma_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}}$ for probabilities.
